step_by_step_reasoning: The architecture shows Snapchat's massive-scale messaging pipeline on AWS. First, we identify user actors: iOS and Android clients. The backend is deployed on a large Amazon EKS fleet (900+ clusters using Graviton). We represent each microservice (GW, MEDIA, MCS, FRIEND GRAPH, and SNAP DB) as an ElasticKubernetesService node since they run inside EKS. For the upload flow (Flow 0), iOS requests hit the Gateway, which directs media uploads to the Media service; this service persists content to S3 via CloudFront and queries the Friend Graph service. For the retrieval and delivery flow (Flow 1), the Messaging Connection Service (MCS) coordinates push delivery by fetching persistent connection metadata from ElastiCache, updating messaging states in SnapDB (a custom caching layer backed by DynamoDB), and pushing the message to the Android client, which then retrieves media from CloudFront.

graph.name: Snapchat High-Scale Messaging Architecture
graph.notes: Handles over 300M+ daily active users and billions of snaps. Utilizes 900+ EKS clusters, many with over 1000+ instances running Graviton to reduce cost and latency. DynamoDB stores 400TB of metadata and runs nightly scans at 2 billion rows per minute.

nodes.name: iOS App Client
nodes.notes: iOS mobile client initiating snap uploads and requests.

nodes.name: Android App Client
nodes.notes: Android mobile client receiving real-time snap deliveries and pulling media content.

nodes.name: EKS Gateway
nodes.notes: EKS-based API gateway acting as the entry point for incoming client requests.

nodes.name: Media Delivery Service
nodes.notes: Microservice running on EKS responsible for media uploads and validation.

nodes.name: Messaging Connection Service
nodes.notes: Microservice running on EKS that manages active, persistent websocket connections to global clients.

nodes.name: Friend Graph Service
nodes.notes: Microservice running on EKS managing user social graphs and relations.

nodes.name: SnapDB
nodes.notes: A custom database abstraction and caching layer built to handle transactions, TTLs, and ephemeral data.

nodes.name: Amazon CloudFront
nodes.notes: CDN used for low-latency media delivery and uploads near the recipients.

nodes.name: Amazon S3
nodes.notes: Object storage bucket for persistent snap media files.

nodes.name: Amazon ElastiCache
nodes.notes: Stores active connection mappings, server IDs, and metadata for rapid connection routing.

nodes.name: Amazon DynamoDB
nodes.notes: Persistent NoSQL store holding 400TB+ of snap metadata, supporting massive nightly parallel scans.

edges.notes: iOS client initiates snap sending via the EKS Gateway.
Gateway routes the media request to the Media Delivery Service.
Media service uploads the content to CloudFront to locate it closer to recipients.
CloudFront persists and backs up the media files to Amazon S3.
Media service verifies recipient associations and social graphs.
Messaging Connection Service looks up active server IDs and connections from ElastiCache.
MCS synchronizes metadata states with SnapDB.
SnapDB reads and flushes persistent metadata transactions back to Amazon DynamoDB.
MCS pushes instant messaging events to the Android recipient over a persistent connection.
Android client retrieves the corresponding snap media from CloudFront using the media ID.
